lessons.title: el tiempo — weather, and a word that means two things at once
lessons.gloss: weather — el tiempo means BOTH "time" and "weather"; hace calor/frío/sol reuse hacer, but llueve is its OWN dedicated verb, and a callback to the cl-/pl- becomes ll- sound change

segments.text: Ask a Spanish speaker "¿qué tiempo hace?" and you're literally asking "what time does it make?" — because tiempo doesn't distinguish "time" from "weather" the way English does.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart: el tiempo

segments.text: el tiempo = both "time" and "weather" — from Latin tempus, which already covered this same double sense (English kept only the "time" half: temporal, contemporary, tempo). So ¿qué tiempo hace? ("what's the weather like?") is literally "what time does it make?" — context alone tells a Spanish speaker which sense is meant.

blocks.title: The words, taken apart: calor, frío, and sol

segments.text: calor from Latin calor, "heat, warmth" becomes English calorie, caloric.
frío from Latin frigidus, "cold" (with the middle syncopated away over time) becomes English frigid, refrigerate.
sol from Latin sol, "sun," unchanged becomes English solar, solstice, parasol.

You've already met hace calor and hace frío ("it's hot/cold," literally "it makes heat/cold") back when you learned hacer — the same hacer ("to make") that reports weather this way also covers "sunny": hace sol ("it's sunny," literally "it makes sun").

blocks.title: Why it's said this way: llueve uses its own verb

segments.text: Rain breaks the hacer pattern entirely: llueve ("it's raining") comes from its own verb, llover from Latin pluere, "to rain." Recognize that pl- becomes ll- shift? It's the same regular sound change you met with llamar ( from clamāre), llave ( from clāvem), and llama ( from flamma) — Latin cl-, fl-, and pl- clusters all regularly became Spanish ll-. So while calor/frío/sol just need hacer in front of them, rain gets its own dedicated, impersonal verb — much like English's own dedicated "it rains" versus "it is hot."

segments.text: What two things does el tiempo mean, and what Latin word covers both? ("Time" and "weather" — Latin tempus.) Which weather word does NOT use hacer? (Llueve — "it's raining," its own verb llover.) What Latin cluster did llover's ll- come from, and what other word taught you this same sound change? (pl-, the same shift as llamar from clamāre.)
